intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. The notes under each slide explain it, tell you what to remember and warn you where people slip. Work the exercises in pencil, check yourself against the questions, and write your own notes in the space around mine.

sections.title: What Qualitative Research Is & When To Use It
sections.big_idea: Qualitative research studies **meaning, process and context**, and it answers the why and how that numbers cannot.
in_plain_words: Qualitative research works with talk, text, observed behaviour and images to understand how people make sense of their lives. The weakest way to define it is 'not numbers'. The better definition is the question it answers: meaning, process and context. Some qualitative work counts, and some quantitative work interprets.

Match the method to the question. A survey tells you what share of girls drop out after Class 8, and interviews tell you why. When you do not yet know the categories, a closed question hands your own assumptions back to you as data, so qualitative work usually comes first.

Qualitative and quantitative work form a loop: one round supplies categories, the survey sizes them, and the next qualitative round tests whether they held. It gives thick description, depth, context and voice, and it pays for them with prevalence claims. Judge it by depth and rigour.

left.title: Quantitative asks
items: Did the outcome change, by how much?

right.title: Qualitative asks
items: Why did it work or fail?

key_terms.meaning: The systematic study of meaning, process and lived experience in context.
Detailed accounts that capture behaviour together with its context and meaning.
Using qualitative and quantitative work together, often in a loop.
A question with fixed answer categories, which carries the researcher's assumptions.
Participants speaking in their own words and categories.

worked_example.title: Pick the method for each question
worked_example.setup: Four questions from the deck's table.
steps: 'What share of girls drop out after Class 8?' asks how many, so a survey, since qualitative cannot answer it.
'Why do they drop out?' needs interviews, because a survey can only test hypotheses you already have.
'How do families decide, and who decides?' needs interviews and observation.
'What does the community mean by safe?' makes the category itself the object, so it is qualitative.
worked_example.answer: Survey, interviews, interviews with observation, and qualitative work.

mistakes: Defining qualitative research as 'not numbers' and then judging it by statistical standards.
Designing a survey first and commissioning qualitative work afterwards to explain results the instrument distorted.
Using qualitative work to estimate prevalence, track a trend or compare trial arms; it will answer, and the answer will be wrong.
Treating a write-up that gives the reader no way to disagree as thick description.

recall.q: What defines qualitative work, according to the deck?
recall.a: The question it answers: meaning, process and context.

recall.q: Name three situations where qualitative work is the right choice.
recall.a: Any three of: exploring a poorly understood phenomenon, understanding process, hearing marginalised voices, explaining a surprising finding, generating survey instruments, sensitive topics.

recall.q: What does a survey finding of 18% dropout establish, and what can it not?
recall.a: It establishes the scale of the problem but not the reason.

recall.q: What does the deck say when a survey and interviews disagree?
recall.a: The disagreement is the finding.

recall.q: Which standards should qualitative work be judged by?
recall.a: Depth, rigour, saturation, credibility, transferability and a visible audit trail.

sections.title: Paradigms & Approaches
sections.big_idea: Your assumptions about reality and knowledge shape your method, so **state your worldview and pick an approach on purpose**.
in_plain_words: A worldview sits behind every study and has two layers: ontology asks what there is to know, and epistemology asks how we can know it. Methodology and methods sit below them. Most method disputes are ontology disputes argued in the wrong vocabulary.

Positivists see one external reality and treat the researcher as a source of contamination. Interpretivists see reality as socially constructed and make the researcher's influence visible. Critical and pragmatic stances add purposes: exposing power, or answering the question usefully.

Five approaches follow from these choices: grounded theory, phenomenology, ethnography, case study and narrative. Each shapes sampling, data and analysis. Claiming a label you did not follow is the common error.

diagram.caption: five traditions and what each asks

key_terms.meaning: What is there to know; whether empowerment is a thing or a construct.
How we can know it; whether a neutral observer is possible.
Examining how your identity and presence shape the data.
Choosing the next case by what the emerging analysis needs.
Setting aside your own assumptions to centre the participant's world.

worked_example.title: Match the study to an approach
worked_example.setup: Four proposals, each with a central question.
steps: 'What theory explains how widows get pensions?' wants a theory of a process, so grounded theory.
'What is it like to wait for a denied pension?' asks for lived experience, so phenomenology.
'How does this panchayat office work as a culture?' needs prolonged immersion, so ethnography.
'How and why did this one SHG federation succeed?' is a bounded unit with many sources, so a case study.
worked_example.answer: Grounded theory, phenomenology, ethnography and case study.

mistakes: Claiming grounded theory for coding a fixed set of interviews, which is thematic analysis.
Treating a positivist reviewer's dislike of a reflexive account as a flaw in your work, without naming your worldview.
Running rapid ethnography and claiming what prolonged immersion delivers.
Choosing a case without saying why, or dressing up convenience as theoretical selection.

recall.q: What do ontology and epistemology ask?
recall.a: What there is to know, and how we can know it.

recall.q: How do positivists and interpretivists differ on bias?
recall.a: Positivists treat the researcher's presence as error; interpretivists treat it as a condition of access to document.

recall.q: What does grounded theory require?
recall.a: Interleaved collection and analysis, theoretical sampling and constant comparison until categories saturate.

recall.q: What is the typical n for phenomenology?
recall.a: Often under 10, interviewed at length.

recall.q: What do reviewers ask of a case study?
recall.a: Why this case.

sections.title: Designing a Qualitative Study
sections.big_idea: Flexibility is not improvisation: **decide the question, approach, participants, methods and analysis plan before fieldwork**.
in_plain_words: A clear design makes a study rigorous and defensible. Settle the research question, the approach, who is information-rich, which methods and why, how coding will work and what ethics demands. The analysis plan gets skipped most often, and deciding how to code after 40 transcripts exist is how projects stall.

Good questions start with how or what and let the answer surprise you. A conceptual framework maps concepts and expected links as a working guide, and it should change when fieldwork contradicts it. Build rigour into the design through triangulation, negative cases, an audit trail and reflexivity.
Emergent design means documented change, and a plan still exists. Mixed-methods designs add a sequence of strands, and each design carries a scheduling failure of its own that the second table lists.

nodes.label: Research question
nodes.sub: what we do not yet know

diagram.caption: the four design decisions in order

key_terms.meaning: A working map of key concepts and expected relationships.
A design that changes as early data arrive, with every change recorded.
A case that contradicts the emerging story.
Using several sources or methods on one question.
Qualitative first, then a survey built from it.

worked_example.title: Rewrite the weak questions
worked_example.setup: Three weak questions from the deck.
steps: 'How many widows receive pensions?' is countable, so ask 'How do widows go through the claim process?'
'Is the scheme effective?' presumes a shared definition, so ask 'What does the scheme change in daily life?'
'Why don't women use the toilets?' presumes refusal, so ask 'What shapes where women choose to go?'
Test each: what answer would surprise you?
worked_example.answer: Three open questions that start with how or what and presume no answer.

mistakes: Leaving the analysis plan until after the data exist.
Writing a question that contains an accusation, which returns evidence for the accusation.
Keeping a conceptual framework unchanged to the end, which means the fieldwork taught nothing or the learning was not recorded.
Running mixed strands on different timelines so they meet only at the write-up.

recall.q: What are the design elements to decide before fieldwork?
recall.a: Research question, approach, participants, methods, analysis plan and ethics.

recall.q: How do strong qualitative questions usually begin?
recall.a: With how, what or in what way, rarely with how many.

recall.q: What must be recorded under emergent design?
recall.a: Every change and the reason for it.

recall.q: What are the four mixed-methods designs?
recall.a: Exploratory, explanatory, convergent and embedded.

recall.q: What should you keep for explanatory designs?
recall.a: A linking identifier and consent to recontact.

sections.title: Sampling
sections.big_idea: Qualitative sampling is **purposive**: choose the cases that are information-rich, and write down why.
in_plain_words: Probability sampling selects for representativeness and supports estimates about a population. Purposive sampling selects for information richness and supports claims about a process or concept. It is not the same as convenience; every choice needs a stated reason tied to the question.

Strategies include maximum variation, typical, extreme, critical, homogeneous and confirming or disconfirming cases. Theoretical sampling lets analysis choose who is next, and snowball sampling reaches hidden groups through referral chains while risking confidentiality.

Saturation tells you when to stop, but it must be argued with a stated rule. Small samples support analytic generalisation to theory, and transferability puts the judgement on the reader. Sizes are rough guides for a budget.

key_terms.meaning: Selecting participants for what they can teach you about the phenomenon.
Spanning diversity deliberately to find patterns across difference.
Participants refer others who fit the study.
New interviews stop yielding new codes, themes or insights.
Generalising to theory and concepts; the claim never reaches a population.

worked_example.title: Argue saturation credibly
worked_example.setup: The deck's best saturation claim: after interview 14 no new codes appeared, and three further interviews were run to confirm.
steps: State the rule: no new codes after interview 14.
Test the judgement with confirming interviews: 14 + 3 = 17 interviews in all.
Say what saturation covers, for example saturation for X but not Y.
Compare with a bare 'we reached saturation', which proves nothing alone.
worked_example.answer: 17 interviews, with a stated stopping rule, a test of it and its scope.

mistakes: Writing 'they were available' as the reason for a selection.
Starting a snowball from one network, so the sample stays inside one circle.
Confirming participation to the person who referred them.
Claiming saturation without a stated rule or evidence that you tested it.

recall.q: What does purposive sampling select for?
recall.a: Information richness.

recall.q: When is maximum variation the safest default?
recall.a: In applied work, because patterns surviving deliberate difference transfer best.

recall.q: Why can theoretical sampling not be pre-specified?
recall.a: The next participant is chosen by what the last ones revealed.

recall.q: What is the indicative range for a focused interview study?
recall.a: 5 to 25 interviews.

recall.q: What is information power?
recall.a: The narrower the question, the more specific the sample and the stronger the analysis, the fewer participants you need.

sections.title: In-Depth & Semi-Structured Interviews
sections.big_idea: The semi-structured interview balances **comparability with depth**, and probing is where depth comes from.
in_plain_words: A semi-structured interview follows an open guide of themes but is free to follow up, reorder and probe. It differs from a questionnaire read aloud, from an unprepared chat and from a chance to confirm what you expect. Second interviews often produce the best material.

Keep the guide to a page: easy grand-tour questions first, general before specific, sensitive material late and a closing question about what you should have asked. Ask open, neutral questions and probe with silence, echo, elaboration, specifying and contrast.

The field shapes the data. Who is in the room, the venue, the interviewer's caste and the language all matter, and power asymmetries distort answers. Budget time for transcription and keep key local terms in the original.

diagram.caption: a one-page interview guide, top to bottom

key_terms.meaning: An interview around an open guide, free to probe and reorder.
An easy, concrete opener such as 'tell me about a typical day'.
A prompt that deepens an answer without leading it.
A question that supplies the answer.
The sense of safety that lets people talk.

worked_example.title: Budget a 10-interview study
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: ten one-hour interviews. The deck says to budget an hour of preparation and four to six hours of transcription and notes per interview hour.
steps: Per interview, the low case is 1 + 4 = 5 hours and the high case is 1 + 6 = 7 hours.
Across ten interviews: 10 × 5 = 50 hours low and 10 × 7 = 70 hours high.
Add the interview time itself: 10 + 50 = 60 hours low and 10 + 70 = 80 hours high.
Translate in the original language first and the work roughly doubles.

mistakes: Writing a forty-question guide, which turns into a questionnaire in the room.
Asking 'Don't you find the scheme helpful?' or any other leading question.
Probing with 'why' too often, which demands justification.
Omitting who else was in the room from the transcript header.

recall.q: What is the closing question?
recall.a: 'Is there anything I should have asked?'

recall.q: Which probe is the most underused?
recall.a: Silence.

recall.q: Where do interpreters fit?
recall.a: They are briefed as research partners and never treated as translation machines.

recall.q: Which three terms carry meaning no single English word holds?
recall.a: Izzat, majboori and sharam.

recall.q: What do you do with a guide before fieldwork?
recall.a: Test it in the actual interview language with someone who will argue with you.

sections.title: Focus Group Discussions
sections.big_idea: A focus group produces **collective, public data**, so compose it carefully and analyse the interaction.
in_plain_words: An FGD is a facilitated discussion of typically 6 to 10 people. It shows publicly sayable norms, live disagreement, the group's own vocabulary and silences. It is a different kind of data and offers no cheaper route to eight interviews.

Compose groups to be homogeneous on the axis that matters, because mixing genders, castes, employers and workers or officials and beneficiaries silences the less powerful. Logistics decide who comes: time of day, venue, childcare and how the invitation is made.

The facilitator sets ground rules, asks and steps back, and draws out the quiet without naming them. A note-taker records what the transcript loses. Analyse the group as the unit, and skip the method for sensitive topics.

key_terms.meaning: A facilitated discussion among about 6 to 10 people on a focused topic.
Similarity on the axis that bears on your topic.
False consensus, such as agreement after one confident early answer.
Giving the 'correct' public answer.
The second staff member who records dynamics.

worked_example.title: Size an FGD plan
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: two audience segments, women-only and men-only, using the deck's ranges of 3 to 6 groups per segment and 6 to 10 participants per group.
steps: Groups: 2 × 3 = 6 at the low end and 2 × 6 = 12 at the high end.
Participants at the low end: 6 × 6 = 36.
Participants at the high end: 12 × 10 = 120.
Each group needs a facilitator and a note-taker, so plan staff to match.

mistakes: Reporting an FGD as a head-count such as 'eight of ten said'.
Mixing castes or genders in one group and treating the quiet as agreement.
Inviting through the sarpanch only, or by written invitation to non-literate participants.
Running an FGD on violence, debt or caste shame because it was cheaper.

recall.q: What group size does the deck give for an FGD?
recall.a: Typically 6 to 10 people.

recall.q: How long should an FGD run?
recall.a: 60 to 90 minutes.

recall.q: How should a quiet participant be drawn in?
recall.a: Address a side of the room and avoid naming the person.

recall.q: Why can confidentiality not be guaranteed in a group?
recall.a: Participants may repeat what they heard; it can only be requested.

recall.q: What should you use for sensitive topics?
recall.a: Private in-depth interviews.

sections.title: Observation & Ethnography
sections.big_idea: Observation shows **what people do** as well as what they say, and field notes are the data.
in_plain_words: People report the norm, because the norm is what they think you ask about, and routine practice is hard to describe from inside. Observation captures practice, routine and the taken-for-granted. The gap is rarely dishonesty.

Choose a role on the spectrum from complete observer to complete participant. Most development fieldwork sits in the middle: openly a researcher but participating enough to understand. Covert participation is rarely justifiable and ongoing consent in public settings is hard.

Write field notes the same day, in three layers (descriptive, reflective, personal), and keep a reflexive journal from day one. Name your positionality, whether insider, outsider or both, and use mixed teams to compare what each was told.

diagram.caption: degrees of participation, from detached to immersed

key_terms.meaning: Taking part in a group's daily life while systematically recording it.
Dated, located records of what you saw, written the same day.
A separate record of how your presence shapes the data.
Your standing as insider, outsider or both.
A concrete, factual account of what happened.

worked_example.title: Budget field note time
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: four observation sessions of three hours each. The deck says an hour observed needs an hour or more to write up.
steps: Observed hours: 4 × 3 = 12.
Minimum writing time at one hour per observed hour: 12 × 1 = 12 hours.
Total minimum time: 12 + 12 = 24 hours.
If writing takes longer than an hour per hour, the total rises.

mistakes: Writing notes days later, when detail has gone.
Mixing observation and interpretation on the same line.
Writing a positionality statement only at the end.
Treating a short rapid ethnography as equal to prolonged immersion.

recall.q: What are the three note layers?
recall.a: Descriptive, reflective and personal.

recall.q: Which participation role is rarely justifiable?
recall.a: Complete participant, in covert form.

recall.q: What must a transcript header record?
recall.a: Who else was in the room.

recall.q: What is the insider's blind spot?
recall.a: The taken-for-granted.

recall.q: How do mixed teams use positionality?
recall.a: Different researchers interview different groups and compare what each was told.

sections.title: Participatory & Visual Methods
sections.big_idea: Participatory methods hand analytical power to communities, but they are **hollow without power to act**.
in_plain_words: Participatory research changes who sets the question, who analyses and who owns the output. Chambers's question, whose reality counts, challenges how knowledge is ordered. The tools follow from taking it seriously. Agree ownership of outputs in writing before fieldwork.

PRA and PLA are facilitated, visual group methods: social and resource maps, transect walks, seasonal calendars, wealth ranking and Venn diagrams. The argument during the exercise is the data, so record it. Optimal ignorance means collecting only what action needs.

Photovoice puts the camera in participants' hands, and the discussion is the method. Visual work needs separate consent for taking, participating and each use. Plan storage and deletion for the DPDP Act, 2023.

left.title: Conventional research
items: Researcher or funder sets the question

right.title: Participatory research
items: Community sets it, at least in part

key_terms.meaning: Participatory Rural Appraisal, later Participatory Learning and Action.
Collect what is needed for action and stop short of everything possible.
A structured walk across a village observing and discussing.
Participants photograph, caption and discuss their own lives.
The community sorts households by its own criteria.

worked_example.title: Which tool surfaces which disagreement?
worked_example.setup: Match each question to a participatory tool from the deck.
steps: Who actually controls the water, whatever the record says? Resource mapping.
When does hunger fall, and does it match the programme calendar? Seasonal calendar.
Which institutions matter and which are merely present? Venn diagram.
What do locals mean by poor? Wealth ranking, which is the most revealing and the most sensitive.
worked_example.answer: Resource map, seasonal calendar, Venn diagram and wealth ranking.

mistakes: Running a mapping exercise on the morning of a field visit and never revisiting it.
Routing the transect walk through the dominant-caste centre only.
Treating Photovoice images as findings without the participants' own account.
Treating consent to be photographed as consent to publication.

recall.q: Who is associated with PRA?
recall.a: Robert Chambers and the IDS at Sussex.

recall.q: What does 'handing over the stick' mean?
recall.a: Participants draw and rank; you do not hold the pen.

recall.q: What makes participation hollow?
recall.a: No decision attached, or outputs that leave with the researcher.

recall.q: What are the Photovoice stages?
recall.a: Briefing, shooting, selection, captioning and discussion, and use.

recall.q: What question tests a participatory exercise?
recall.a: What happens after.

sections.title: Data Management & Coding
sections.big_idea: Manage the data before you analyse it, then code with **a codebook that states each code's boundary**.
in_plain_words: Qualitative projects accumulate recordings, transcripts, notes, photos and consent forms. Use participant codes in file names, keep a master key separately and encrypted, agree one folder structure, test backups and delete recordings as consent promised.

Transcription and translation involve analytic choices. Verbatim keeps pauses and overlaps, cleaned transcripts keep meaning, and summary notes cannot support quotation. Budget four to six hours per audio hour and more across languages.

Coding tags segments with short labels, inductively from the data or deductively from a framework. A codebook gives each code a definition, an inclusion rule, a boundary and an example. Software organises and counts but never does the thinking.

diagram.caption: four kinds of code with the deck's examples

key_terms.meaning: The separate, encrypted link between participant codes and identities.
Every word, pause and overlap.
A dictionary of codes: definition, inclusion rule, boundary, example.
A label taken from the participant's own words.
Software that organises, retrieves and counts coded segments.

worked_example.title: Estimate transcription time
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: twelve hours of interview audio, using the deck's four to six hours per audio hour.
steps: Low case: 12 × 4 = 48 hours.
High case: 12 × 6 = 72 hours.
Translation across languages adds more, and doubles the work if you transcribe the original first.
Write the budget into the plan before fieldwork.

mistakes: Putting names in file names or storing the master key beside the data.
Cleaning a transcript so that a long pause before a hard answer disappears.
Leaving the 'when not to' line out of a code definition.
Reporting the software's frequency table as a finding.

recall.q: What goes in a filename?
recall.a: A participant code, never a name.

recall.q: What does a codebook entry contain?
recall.a: Name, definition, when to apply, when not to and an example.

recall.q: What is the test of a hybrid coding approach that worked?
recall.a: At least one important finding sits outside the original framework.

recall.q: Which software is free and open-source?
recall.a: Taguette.

recall.q: What does CAQDAS not do?
recall.a: Decide what a code means or interpret the network.

sections.title: Thematic Analysis & Interpretation
sections.big_idea: A theme is **a constructed pattern of meaning** that answers the question, and analysis goes beyond sorting.
in_plain_words: Thematic analysis, systematised by Braun and Clarke, moves through six phases: familiarisation, generating codes, searching for themes, reviewing themes, defining themes and writing up. The phases are recursive, and phase four, checking every extract against its theme, is what separates analysis from sorting.

Themes mirroring the interview guide show that the data were sorted. Frequency reflects your sampling and guide, so a rare code can carry the key insight. Interpretation climbs from describing to interpreting, explaining and theorising, and asks what is absent.

Triangulation, negative cases and careful quotes give the analysis its strength. Use quotes to illustrate a theme and never to prove prevalence, show the full range of positions, and attribute each one by code and relevant attributes.

diagram.caption: six phases, revisited as understanding deepens

key_terms.meaning: A pattern of meaning that answers the research question, constructed by the analyst.
A grouping of codes inside a theme.
Data that does not fit the emerging story.
Converging data, method, investigator or theory.
A quote chosen to show a theme, which says nothing about how common it is.

worked_example.title: Rewrite a percentage claim
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a code appears in 12 of 15 interviews, and the draft says '80% said'.
steps: Compute the figure: 12 ÷ 15 = 0.8, which the draft calls 80%.
The percentage imports a claim the method cannot support, from a sample chosen for richness.
Rewrite: 'Most participants described the journey as the barrier.'
Define 'most' once in the methods section and do not count.
worked_example.answer: Replace '80% said' with a defined word such as 'most'.

mistakes: Naming themes after interview guide sections.
Skipping phase four so themes go unchecked against extracts.
Letting 'most-mentioned wins' discard the single account that explains how exclusion works.
Stopping at a set of headed quote collections and calling it analysis.

recall.q: Who systematised thematic analysis?
recall.a: Virginia Braun and Victoria Clarke, 2006.

recall.q: What are the four levels of interpretation?
recall.a: Describe, interpret, explain and theorise.

recall.q: What should you do when you find no negative cases?
recall.a: Look harder, then say you looked and how.

recall.q: What does frequency tell you?
recall.a: Where the corpus is dense and which codes are well evidenced.

recall.q: What should quotes do?
recall.a: Illustrate a theme, show the range and carry attribution by code.

sections.title: Trustworthiness, Ethics & Reading
sections.big_idea: Qualitative rigour is **trustworthiness**: credibility, transferability, dependability and confirmability, backed by ethics that go deep.
in_plain_words: Lincoln and Guba offered four criteria parallel to validity, generalisability, reliability and objectivity. Applying statistical validity or effect size to qualitative work is a category error. Only credibility concerns the analysis itself; the others rest on what you wrote down.

Techniques that build credibility include member checking, triangulation, prolonged engagement, peer debriefing and negative-case analysis, each with a limit. An audit trail of dated decisions and a reflexive journal support dependability and confirmability.

Ethics are heavier because the work goes deep: informed and ongoing consent, confidentiality, do no harm, voluntariness and reciprocity. South Asian fieldwork adds oral consent, gatekeeper pressure, fragile anonymity and the DPDP Act, 2023.

key_terms.meaning: Lincoln and Guba's framework for rigour in qualitative research.
Taking findings back to participants to verify them.
A record of every methodological and analytic decision.
A colleague challenges your interpretation.
Returning findings in a usable form.

worked_example.title: Match the technique to the criterion
worked_example.setup: Four things you did in a study.
steps: You compared interview, observation and document findings on one issue: triangulation, which builds credibility.
You described the setting thickly so readers elsewhere could judge fit: transferability.
You kept dated memos and a codebook history: dependability, through the audit trail.
You kept a reflexive journal and traced findings to the data: confirmability.

mistakes: Asking a participant to validate a raw transcript instead of an interpretation.
Treating a signed form as consent when understanding has not happened.
Reconstructing the audit trail from memory at the end.
Promising benefits the research cannot deliver.

recall.q: Which criterion is the parallel of internal validity?
recall.a: Credibility.

recall.q: Which of the four criteria is about the analysis itself?
recall.a: Credibility.

recall.q: What should you have before an interview on violence or bereavement?
recall.a: A referral route.

recall.q: What does the deck say about the DPDP Act, 2023?
recall.a: Its duties apply from 13 May 2027, so plan storage and deletion now.

recall.q: Which book does the deck suggest first for analysing data this month?
recall.a: Braun and Clarke (2006).

notes.2: Use the agenda to see where the course moves from ideas to methods. Sections 1 to 3 cover questions, paradigms and design, sections 4 to 8 cover sampling and the field methods, and sections 9 to 11 cover analysis, rigour and ethics. Read first the section for the method you plan to use.
notes.4: Hold on to this definition: qualitative research is defined by the question it answers, which is meaning, process and context. 'Not numbers' is the weakest definition, because some qualitative work counts and some quantitative work interprets. Use the table to see what each type of data is **analysed for**.
notes.5: Match the method to the question before you plan anything. The last row of the table is the one practitioners miss: when you do not yet know the categories, a **closed question hands your assumptions back to you as data**. That is why qualitative work usually comes first.
notes.6: Use the second table as a test of your own project. Choose qualitative work when the phenomenon is poorly understood, a result needs explaining, or you are designing a survey. The mirror list matters as much: **never estimate prevalence or compare trial arms** with it.
notes.7: Read this as a loop. A survey sizes the problem, interviews find mechanisms, a second survey counts them and a programme tests an answer. Where survey and interviews disagree, **the disagreement is the finding**. High satisfaction beside stories of avoidance usually means the instrument measured compliance.
notes.8: Thick description records enough context for a reader to check your reading. In the wink example the movement is identical at every layer, and the meaning changes with relationship, local gestures and presence. If a reader has no way to disagree, you have **assertion with quotes attached**.
notes.9: Each strength carries its cost: depth means a small n, and adaptability means a flexible design. You cannot keep one and discard the other. A bigger sample adds shallow interviews and no new claim, so do not try to fix qualitative work by **scaling it up**.
notes.10: Prepare for the objection 'your sample is only fifteen'. The calm answer is that fifteen was chosen for information richness and never to estimate a proportion. Judge the work by depth, saturation, credibility, transferability and an audit trail. Sample size and response rate are **the wrong standards**.
notes.12: Name your worldview in the write-up. Ontology asks what there is to know, epistemology how we can know it, methodology how you go about it and methods which tools you use. Most method disputes are ontology disputes, and **your stated position tells readers which quality criteria apply**.
notes.13: Compare the poles row by row. They disagree about bias: one treats the researcher's presence as contamination, the other as a condition of access to document. That is why **reflexivity counts as rigour on one side** and is irrelevant on the other.
notes.14: Two more stances: critical and pragmatic. The table's last column asks who judges success: other researchers, readers, those the work serves, or whoever has to act. If research is meant to contribute to change, **extracting data and leaving is a design failure**. Name your stance.
notes.15: Choose the approach on purpose, because it shapes sampling, data and analysis. The two tables give each tradition's central question, typical n and output. The label matters most when you write up. A common error is claiming grounded theory for what is really **thematic analysis**.
notes.16: Grounded theory interleaves collection and analysis, samples theoretically and compares constantly until categories saturate. Few funded studies can do this because budgets and ethics approvals fix the sample in advance. If yours does, say so and avoid relabelling. The Strauss and Corbin version allows a loose starting framework.
notes.17: Phenomenology asks what an experience is like from the inside, so very small samples are correct. The table contrasts experiential questions with their countable versions. **Bracketing** is the central discipline and controversy. Six people interviewed three times give more of what the method needs than sixty interviewed once.
notes.18: Ethnography needs months of presence, participation, daily field notes and patience with the early weeks. Budget several hours of writing for each day observed. 'Rapid ethnography' in development practice is a **different method with the same name** and should not claim what prolonged immersion delivers.
notes.19: A case study needs four decisions: what the case is, its boundaries, single or multiple, and **why this case**. Reviewers ask the last and studies dodge it. Convenience is legitimate if stated. Pick Yin's design with propositions or Stake's interpretation of a particular, and stay consistent.
notes.21: Fix the design before you collect anything, including the analysis plan, which is the item that gets skipped. Deciding how to code after 40 transcripts exist is how projects stall. Flexibility applies to the sample and the questions, and **emergent design means documented change**, with a plan still in place.
notes.22: Compare strong and weak questions. Strong ones begin with how or what and let the answer surprise you. Check the rewrites in the table. The third row is the trap: a question containing an accusation returns evidence for it. Ask **what answer would surprise you**.
notes.23: Treat the conceptual framework as a working map of concepts and expected connections that fieldwork will revise. A framework that never changes is a warning sign. Keep the early version, because showing how it moved between proposal and write-up is a **convincing piece of audit trail**.
notes.24: Build rigour in at design, since each item here is nearly free then and nearly impossible to retrofit. Choose triangulation sources, name who could contradict you, set up the audit trail and start a reflexive journal on day one. Plan **negative-case sampling hardest**, because purposive sampling drifts towards confirmation.
notes.25: Emergent design shifts the burden from planning to documentation. Record which guide question changed and why, the analytic reason for each new participant, dated code changes and each version of the question. Ethics committees expect a fixed protocol, so **specify the range of permitted adaptation** up front.
notes.26: This chart is an illustrative schematic of the trade between qualitative depth and quantitative breadth. The point is the trade: twelve detailed interviews, well chosen and analysed, can teach more than a thousand thin ones. Do not read numbers off the chart, because the deck labels it illustrative.
notes.27: Pick the mixed design by sequence and purpose, then read the failure in the second table. Each failure is a **scheduling failure**, caused by two strands run by different people on different timelines. For explanatory designs, keep a linking identifier and consent to recontact at the survey stage.
notes.29: Purposive sampling selects people who can teach you about the phenomenon, so each selection needs a written reason tied to the question. 'They were available' weakens the study. **Write the rationale as you go**, because one reconstructed afterwards always reads as post-hoc justification.
notes.30: Pick the strategy by what you need: variation, the norm, outliers, a decisive case, a group that can talk freely, or cases that test your theory. **Maximum variation is the safest default** for applied work. Strategies combine, for instance variation across sites with homogeneous groups within each.
notes.31: Theoretical sampling chooses the next participant by what your analysis lacks: analyse, spot a gap, select a case that probes it, repeat. It cannot be pre-specified, which clashes with most ethics protocols. Seek approval for **a range and criteria**, then report the actual sequence and reasons.
notes.32: Use snowball sampling for hidden populations that appear on no list, and start from several unconnected seeds. **Never confirm participation to the referrer**, because with stigmatised groups the fact of taking part can itself be the harmful disclosure. Respondent-driven sampling is a separate, heavier method.
notes.33: Saturation means new interviews stop yielding new codes, but it is a judgement and not a number. In the table, 'we reached saturation' proves nothing alone, while **a stated stopping rule** and confirming interviews do. Braun and Clarke say it sits awkwardly in thematic analysis.
notes.34: This curve is illustrative: new themes per extra interview taper off, and by around interview 12 to 16 little new emerges. The exact point depends on scope, diversity and the breadth of your question. Use it to picture saturation and **never to set a sample size**.
notes.35: Qualitative studies seek analytic generalisation, to theory and concepts, in place of statistical generalisation to a population. Answer 'only 15' by describing the context thickly so that readers elsewhere can judge fit. **Transferability puts that judgement on the reader.**
notes.36: Treat the ranges as starting points for a budget. Interview studies run 5 to 25 interviews, focus groups 3 to 6 per segment, and phenomenology often under 10. A study that stops at exactly the proposed number has let the proposal do the analysis. **Information power** is the better framing.
notes.38: The semi-structured interview rests on a flexible guide, so it is comparable and still follows the person. Work through the table of what it is not. Budget one hour of preparation and four to six hours of transcription and notes per interview hour: **studies fail on that arithmetic**.
notes.39: Choose the interview type by how much you need to compare. Structured is near a survey, semi-structured fits most studies, and unstructured suits life histories. If your finding is 'across these fifteen women, three patterns recur', you need shared structure. A good hybrid uses **the same three opening questions**.
notes.40: Build a guide of themes on one page and avoid a script of 40 questions. Start with easy grand-tour questions, go from general to specific, keep sensitive topics until rapport exists and close by asking what you should have asked. The closing question often yields **the most useful sentence**.
notes.41: Compare the leading, double-barrelled, jargon and blame-implying questions with their rewrites. Requests like 'walk me through the last time' produce detail and sequence. Test the guide in the actual interview language, since a question can be **fine in English and leading in translation**.
notes.42: Probe to deepen an answer without leading it. Silence is the most underused probe, and three or four seconds often produces the qualification or the real reason. Use echo, elaboration, specifying and contrast as the table shows. Go easy on 'why', which **demands justification**.
notes.43: People talk when they feel safe, so plan the setting deliberately. The table shows how a mother-in-law's presence, an office venue, a different-caste interviewer or a gatekeeper's choice changes the data. **Record who else was in the room** in the transcript header.
notes.44: Treat the interview as an unequal exchange and name the asymmetries. Researchers linked to a programme hear complaints or praise, class gaps produce deference and hopes of benefit tilt accounts. Say plainly at the start **what the research can and cannot deliver**. Survey fatigue is data about the research economy.
notes.45: Interview in the participant's language and brief any interpreter as a research partner. Each translation choice in the table has a cost, and each is an analytic decision. Keep words like izzat, majboori and sharam in the original beside a gloss, because **losing them loses the analysis**.
notes.47: An FGD produces collective, public data: norms, live disagreement, group vocabulary and silences. It is a different kind of data from eight interviews, and treating it as individual data is **the commonest analytic error**. When a topic raised twice draws no response, that silence is a finding.
notes.48: Use an FGD for what a group produces together: shared norms, live debate and ideas that one comment sparks in another, plus efficient coverage of several voices. Every item here concerns the group as a whole. If you need individual experience, slide 53 says to **use interviews** instead.
notes.49: Compose groups to be homogeneous on the axis that matters for your topic, such as gender, caste or employment. Mixing men and women, castes, employers and workers or officials and beneficiaries silences the less powerful. Run parallel groups, because **the difference between them is a finding**.
notes.50: Logistics are sampling decisions in disguise. Time of day, venue, childcare and how the invitation is made each decide who can be in the room. Plan 6 to 10 participants, 60 to 90 minutes and two staff. **Record who was invited, who came and who did not.**
notes.51: Learn the five facilitator moves: ground rules, ask then stop talking, bring in the quiet, contain the dominant, summarise and check. Address a side of the room instead of naming a quiet person. **Confidentiality in a group can only be requested**, so say that at the start.
notes.52: Ask the note-taker to record what a transcript loses: speaking order, who stayed silent, nods and discomfort, and where the room split. A transcript alone is close to unusable for FGD analysis. Probe **false consensus** after one confident early answer by asking whether everyone sees it that way.
notes.53: Skip the FGD for violence, debt, sexuality or caste shame, for individual experience, where power gaps would silence people, and where participants know each other and will meet again. In a village **what is said outlasts the study**. Be honest if budget drove the choice.
notes.54: Analyse an FGD by its interaction, with the group as the unit. Report 'the group converged' or 'this was contested' and avoid 'eight of ten said', because participants heard each other first and are **not independent**. Treat silence as a finding about what could not be said.
notes.56: Observation captures practice, routine and the taken-for-granted that interviews rarely reach. People report the norm because that is what they think you ask about, and routine is hard to describe from inside. The table pairs **reported with observed practice**. The gap is rarely dishonesty.
notes.57: Choose your role on the participation spectrum, from complete observer to complete participant. Most development fieldwork sits in the middle two rows. Ask whether everyone present knows who you are. **Covert participation is rarely justifiable**, and in public settings ongoing consent needs a stated approach.
notes.58: Participant observation means taking part in a group's daily life while systematically recording it, over time. Sitting through gram sabha meetings month after month shows the **workarounds, hierarchies and informal rules** that no document records. It is the core method of ethnography.
notes.59: Treat field notes as your data. Jot brief scratch notes discreetly, write full notes the same day, separate observation from interpretation, record the mundane and date and locate every entry. Budget **an hour or more of writing per hour observed**, since seating and routine are often the finding.
notes.60: Keep three layers in your notes: descriptive for what happened, reflective for what it might mean and personal for your feelings and doubts. Distinct layers let you later separate **evidence from interpretation from your own bias**. Mark each entry's layer on the page.
notes.61: Reflexivity means examining how your gender, caste, class, language and institution shape what people show and tell you. The table shows what each attribute opens and closes. It is a rigour requirement. Keep a **reflexive journal from day one**, since a statement written at the end is only recollection.
notes.62: Name your positionality as insider, outsider or both. Insiders get trust faster but miss the taken-for-granted, while outsiders notice more and work harder for trust. Almost everyone is partly both, and it shifts by topic. **Mixed teams can compare what each researcher was told.**
notes.64: Participatory research changes who sets the question, who analyses and who owns outputs. Chambers's question, whose reality counts, challenges how knowledge is ordered, and the tools follow from taking it seriously. **Agree ownership of maps and rankings in writing** before fieldwork, since afterwards is too late.
notes.65: PRA and PLA are facilitated, visual group methods that let communities, including non-literate people, analyse their own conditions. Keep the principles in mind: hand over the stick, collect only what action needs, triangulate across groups and use tangible materials. Collecting everything rebuilds **the extractive survey PRA opposed**.
notes.66: Choose a tool by the disagreement you want surfaced. Social maps show who is counted, resource maps who controls water, calendars when hunger falls, wealth ranking local poverty criteria and Venn diagrams which institutions matter. **The argument during the exercise is the data**, so assign someone to record it.
notes.67: On a transect walk, decide who chooses the route, who walks with you, when you walk and where you stop, because each default pulls towards the village centre. Route it through Dalit and Adivasi tolas, and **walk it more than once** with different companions.
notes.68: A community-drawn map is valuable as a record, and the debate while drawing is often where the insight lives. Draw on the ground with sticks, seeds and chalk, include what matters to residents, and **record both the product and the conversation**.
notes.69: In Photovoice, participants photograph their own lives, then choose images, caption and discuss them. The discussion is the analysis and the photographs are the prompt. Brief on consent, safety and what not to photograph, and **agree in advance where images will be used**, for how long and with whose consent.
notes.70: Participation is only as good as the power behind it. It holds when groups are separated and facilitated, findings return to the community and there is power to act on the result. It is hollow when outputs leave with the researcher. **Test it by what happens afterwards.**
notes.71: Treat consent to be photographed, consent to participate and consent to each use as separate. Blurring is a decision, a face cannot be anonymised and a circulating image cannot be recalled. The deck says the **DPDP Act, 2023** applies to identifiable digital data from 13 May 2027, so plan storage and deletion now.
notes.73: Manage your data before you analyse it. Use participant codes in file names, keep the master key separately and encrypted, set one folder structure, test backups and delete recordings as the consent promised. Transcripts identify people through life stories, so **access control matters more** here than in survey work.
notes.74: Choose a transcription style that fits the analysis: verbatim for fine discourse work, cleaned for most thematic analysis, summary notes only for the gist. Cleaning removes hesitation, which can be **evidence of how hard an answer was**. Budget four to six hours per audio hour, more across languages.
notes.75: Decide early whether to translate live or transcribe the original first. Original-then-translate preserves nuance and roughly doubles the work. Keep key terms in the original with a gloss, have a second person check sensitive passages and record who translated what. **Every translation decision is an analytic decision.**
notes.76: Coding means tagging segments with short labels so you can gather and compare every instance of an idea. The table lists descriptive, in vivo, process and emotion codes. Use in vivo codes early to stay in participants' categories. A coded corpus is **organised but has no conclusion yet**.
notes.77: Pick your coding direction. Inductive codes emerge from the data, and deductive codes come from a framework you bring. Most real projects are hybrid. Test yours by asking whether **at least one important finding sits outside the starting framework**. If none does, the inductive half did not happen.
notes.78: A codebook gives each code a name, a one-sentence definition, an inclusion rule, a boundary against the nearest code and a real example. **The 'when not to' line makes two coders agree.** Date it and keep the history of merges, splits and drops as part of your audit trail.
notes.79: Choose software by need. NVivo and ATLAS.ti are paid, Dedoose is a subscription, Taguette is free and a spreadsheet works for small studies. CAQDAS **organises and counts but never thinks for you**. Beware the frequency table, the most seductive output and the likeliest to lead to counts reported as findings.
notes.81: A theme is a pattern of meaning that answers the research question and is constructed by the analyst. Themes that mirror the interview guide are the commonest failure: six guide sections giving six themes means **the data was sorted and not analysed**. Two analysts can reach different, defensible readings.
notes.82: Move through the six phases and expect to loop back, for instance from five to three, and record the movement. The second table shows what each skipped phase costs. **Phase four**, reading every extract against its theme, is what separates thematic analysis from sorting.
notes.83: Follow the example down the tree: four codes about travel and safety roll up into the sub-theme 'the journey' and then into a theme about mobility and safety. **Themes are constructed by the analyst**, and different lenses yield different, equally valid, themes.
notes.84: This chart is illustrative: code frequency across 15 interviews. Counts orient you, but a rare code may carry the key insight. Frequency mostly reflects your sampling and your guide, so never let **'most-mentioned wins'** decide. One account may be the person who explains how exclusion works.
notes.85: Climb four levels: describe, interpret, explain, theorise. Most applied reports stop at describing and call it analysis, so a findings section of headed quote collections has said nothing yet. Also ask what is absent. **What no participant raised**, when you expected it, can be your sharpest finding.
notes.86: Triangulate across data, method, investigator and theory. Where sources converge confidence grows, and where they diverge you learn something new. The panel names four types. Plan two or three sources at design, since **you cannot triangulate against a document you never collected**.
notes.87: Hunt for negative cases, meaning data that does not fit your story, and either revise the explanation or state its conditions. If you find none, look harder, then say you looked and how. Sample for them deliberately. **Perfect coherence in fifteen lives is a warning sign.**
notes.88: Use quotes to illustrate a theme and never to prove prevalence. Show the range, including extracts that cut against you, give enough context to judge your reading and attribute by code. **Combinations of attributes can identify a person** as well as a name. Say how you chose the quotes.
notes.90: Judge qualitative work by trustworthiness. Lincoln and Guba's four criteria are credibility, transferability, dependability and confirmability. Applying effect size or representativeness here is a **category error**. Know both vocabularies, so quantitatively trained colleagues take your findings seriously.
notes.91: Learn the four criteria with the quantitative parallel for each. Only credibility concerns the analysis itself; the other three depend on what you wrote down, which makes them **cheap to secure and easy to lose**. Write all four into your methods section with what you did for each.
notes.92: Use the five techniques and know each one's limit. Member checking can draw flattering endorsements, triangulation can share a bias, prolonged engagement is costly, peer debriefing needs a willing arguer and negative-case analysis needs sampling for it. Take **interpretations** back to participants and keep raw transcripts out of it.
notes.93: The audit trail records every sampling decision, guide revision, codebook change, analytic memo and reflexive entry at the time it happens. Reconstructed afterwards it becomes rationalisation. **Memos are the most valuable and most skipped** item; half a page when an idea forms is often the first draft of a finding.
notes.94: Reflexivity supports confirmability by showing that findings come from the data and do not merely reflect the researcher. Keep a reflexive journal alongside your field notes, so readers can see **both the world and your lens on it**. Start it on day one.
notes.95: Ethics rests on informed consent, confidentiality, do no harm and voluntariness, plus reciprocity. Rapport must never become a tool of extraction. **Have a referral route before you start**, because interviews about violence, debt or bereavement surface active need. The obligation continues after the recorder stops.
notes.96: South Asian fieldwork adds specific duties: oral consent where literacy is low, protection from gatekeeper pressure, coarsened detail in small communities and storage plans for the DPDP Act, 2023. A signed form documents consent, and **understanding is what counts**. Return findings in a usable form and language.
notes.97: Check your draft against five pitfalls: percentages, cherry-picking, stopping at coding, ignoring your influence and over-claiming. Percentages are the commonest in development reporting because donors read them as rigour. If you must show spread, use **defined words** such as 'a few', 'about half' or 'most'.
notes.98: Use these five points as a final check on any plan: match method to question, sample for richness and stop at saturation, aim for depth, be reflexive about power and position, and show rigour as trustworthiness. If a draft breaks one, **return to the matching section**.
notes.99: Start with Braun and Clarke if you have data to analyse this month, since the deck calls it short and the most directly usable. Keep Patton as the reference to own, especially for sampling. Pair the list with **Data Literacy, Research Ethics and MEL Basics 101**.
